newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin foe Rutskoi stages comeback in Russia.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin foe Rutskoi stages comeback in Russia.

text.p: Former Russian vice-president and sworn foe of Boris Yeltsin, Alexander Rutskoi, has won a local election in the central Kursk region by a landslide, seizing the post of governor and staging a remarkable political comeback.

Russian news agencies said Rutskoi, who had only two days to campaign, won 79 percent of the vote in Sunday's election while Vasily Shuteyev, appointed by Yeltsin in 1991 to run the conservative region, got just 18 percent.
The new post gives Rutskoi a place in the Federation Council, the upper chamber of parliament.

Rutskoi was initially banned from running by the local electoral commission which complained he had moved out of his home region long ago. But a court backed Rutskoi's appeal and reinstated him just two days before the poll.
Rutskoi's comeback is certain to infuriate the Kremlin.
Yeltsin chose the Afghan war hero as his running mate in 1991 to win over the votes of reformist communists and the military. The pair easily defeated opponents.
But Rutskoi and Yeltsin drifted apart, both personally and politically, and Rutskoi sided with conservative parliament in its power struggle with the Russian leader.
When Yeltsin, putting the constitution aside, tried to dissolve parliament in September 1993, deputies refused to obey and proclaimed Rutskoi their president.

He led a bloody uprising in Moscow on October 3. Next day, after government tanks shelled the parliament building, Rutskoi and other leading Yeltsin opponents were jailed. The post of vice-president was scrapped under a new constitution.

The new parliament pardoned Rutskoi and others next year and Rutskoi, vowing to stay in politics, formed the nationalist Derzhava movement, which backed communist leader Gennady Zyuganov in the presidential election on July 3.
The Kursk vote was one of several setbacks for the Kremlin in Sunday's regional polls. In the region of Kirov, to the east of Moscow, an opposition member of parliament became governor.

Yeltsin's appointee was defeated in the westernmost enclave of Kaliningrad and there will be a second round of voting in the Pskov region. But the Yeltsin-backed candidate was elected on the far eastern island of Sakhalin.
Regional elections will take place in most of Russia's 89 regions before next February.

Yeltsin's opponents hope a good showing in the regional polls will help them win a majority in the Federation Council, which comprises regional bosses now generally loyal to the Kremlin leader who is preparing for a heart operation.
